idiom_name: require of gems or a Dir.glob'd plugin directory plus explicit registration
implementation_notes: Ruby ships no service-locator metadata, so the pattern is convention: a plugin is a gem or a file, and the host requires it - Jekyll loads every .rb under _plugins and the gems named in its configuration, and RuboCop's plugin API requires declared extension gems and reads a plugin class from each. The contract is duck typing plus an explicit registration call into a host registry, with Gem::Specification and the gem namespace as the packaging and discovery unit, and the classic structure is otherwise hand-written. Because require executes arbitrary code at load time, hosts that run third-party plugins in a hosted environment gate them (Jekyll's safe mode and whitelist) rather than pretending the file is inert.
code_sketch:
module Host
  REGISTRY = {}
  def self.register(kind, &factory) = REGISTRY[kind] = factory
end

Dir.glob("plugins/**/*.rb").sort.each { |path| require File.expand_path(path) }

formatter = Host::REGISTRY.fetch(:csv).call
puts formatter.format(doc)
pitfalls: require is idempotent by path, so editing a plugin under a long-running host changes nothing until the process restarts; load re-executes the file and reopens classes, which is usually worse.
Plugins are required into one global namespace, so constant and method collisions (or monkey patches of core classes) make plugin interactions order-dependent and hard to diagnose.

Filesystem discovery has no ordering or versioning guarantees: Dir.glob order is incidental, and gems can be installed at incompatible versions unless the host pins them (Bundler, config-mediated whitelists).
